editorial.summary: An official-channel, second-person Batman dramatic monologue that opens with graphic vigilante violence, reveals Bruce Wayne’s trauma and compulsive pursuit of invulnerability, then reverses into responsibility, redistribution, medical repair, apology, therapy, friendship and self-love. The complete violent-to-reparative arc is the work: neither the violence nor the final affirmation should be isolated. All characters, assets and events are fiction/intertext rather than David Choe biography or licensed-canon proof. The 152-decision layer repairs names and concepts while leaving damaged martial-arts wording unresolved. No line-level speaker is publisher-labeled, so the public record contains zero named turns.

connections.relationship: The performer places the listener inside a fictional violent scene rather than recounting a verified event.
The opening establishes harm through the opponent’s repeated request to stop.
The bat ears and armored identity reframe the opening as a Batman performance.
Trauma, wealth and control are attached to the fictional character, not Choe biography.
A vow never to be hurt again becomes the engine of compulsive protection.
CrossFit and martial-arts references accumulate as exaggerated attempts at mastery.
Money purchases defenses but cannot resolve fear or grief.
Vehicles, armor and weapons externalize the character’s control fantasy.
Training and vigilance displace softness, play and relationships.
The work names how unresolved hurt reproduces harm.
Punishing others is recognized as a way of continuing to punish oneself.
The character begins giving up the mask, weapons and violent mission.
Connection replaces isolation as a form of safety.
Fantasy wealth is redirected toward medical repair and public benefit.
The character accepts material responsibility for the person harmed.
The monologue acknowledges mistreatment of a caregiver.
Individual and couples therapy appear as fictional repair actions, not medical advice.
The character explicitly stops defining justice as personal violence.
Technical mastery is contrasted with emotional self-knowledge.
The address shifts from accusation toward permission and care.
Worth is separated from protection, punishment and performance.
A comic-character roll call functions as hyperbolic affirmation, not canon evidence.
The dead parents’ pride is consolation inside the fiction.
The outro closes a single work whose beginning and ending should not be separated.

Automatic captions contain 156 long segments, approximately 2,471 words and 20:43 runtime.
This is a performed fictional monologue, not an interview, podcast or factual confession.
Second-person grammar addresses Bruce and the listener inside the dramatic frame.
The bat-mask reveal retroactively establishes the fictional vigilante frame.
Batman/Bruce Wayne and related people, places, wealth, equipment and acts are fictional.
DC references do not prove licensing, approval, ownership, canon status or collaboration.
Wolverine is a cross-publisher Marvel joke/intertext.
The damaged martial-arts list is not silently completed; uncertain names remain unresolved.
CrossFit, Billy Blanks, Tae Bo, jiu-jitsu, Brazilian jiu-jitsu, Gracie, Jeet Kune Do and Bruce Lee are repaired only where context is strong.
The opening includes explicit blood, broken teeth/nose, facial disfigurement, pus and near-death imagery.
Repeated breathing, punching and kicking are performance detail, not instruction.
Fantasy armor, guns, tanks and transforming vehicles are not treated as real assets.
The work explicitly links hurt, invulnerability, victimization and becoming a victimizer.
The work explicitly recognizes punishment of others as self-punishment.
The reversal includes giving up the mask, weapons and vigilantism.
Superman-funded medical care and wealth redistribution are fictional character actions.
Acknowledgment of mistreating Alfred is part of the repair arc.
Individual and couples therapy are fictional narrative choices, not medical recommendations.
The final hero/villain love list is hyperbole, not canon relationship evidence.
The dead parents’ pride is imagined consolation inside the work.
The final isolated caption word is not expanded or invented.
The complete work must remain available uncensored.
Discovery views should foreground structure and context rather than sensational fragments.
